I have got a series of warnings first from nimbleModel() function and then from runMCMC() function, with a Hidden Markov model.
I wonder whether warnings are due to the way I specify priors for latent states ("z").
Here below the code and the errors. I can provide the data out of the list if needed.
Many thanks for your help,
Simone

dim(CH_f)
nind <- dim(CH_f)[1]
nyears <- dim(CH_f)[2]

# Compute the date of first capture for each individual:

for (i in 1:nind){
temp <- 1:nyears
first <- c(first,min(temp[CH_f[i,]>=1]))}

  ps1[7,1:8] <- c(0,0,0,0,0,0,phi,1-phi)
  ps1[8,1:8] <- c(0,0,0,0,0,0,0,1)

  # step 2:
  ps2[1,1:8] <-c(1-psi,psi,0,0,0,0,0,0)
  ps2[2,1:8] <-c(0,1-psi,psi,0,0,0,0,0)
  ps2[3,1:8] <-c(0,0,1,0,0,0,0,0)

messages.body_plain:
Hi everybody,

I am playing around with hmm with continuous signals/observations. I implemented a hmm distribution like in the nimbleEcology package. Now I would like to sample from the hidden states (with the forward-backward algorithm).

My understading is that this is not implemented in the nimbleEcology package.

Any chance I can get intermediate values from the sampling process saved somehow (as in the "generated quantities" option of stan)? Or do I have to write a postprocessing script based on the posterior samples of the high-level parameters and implement this outside of the sampling?

Best,
Patrick

messages.body_plain:
Short answer, Patrick: no, these quantities (samples of the intermediate latent states) are never themselves generated in the calculations done by the nimbleEcology distributions.  The latent states are marginalized over, by propagating a time-sequence of probabilities of each latent state value (at each time period), which are used to calculate the marginal probability of each data observation.

Given what you've said, I think your options are:
- Not use nimbleEcology, and write the latent states into your model, and thereby have samples of them.
- Write a post-processing script, as you mentioned, to generate the desired samples using the posterior samples of the model parameters.
- Modify one of the distributions in nimbleEcology, to use the intermediate probability values to also generate latent states.  Although, from the mechanics of how distributions work in NIMBLE, this would be somewhat awkward, and would (I believe) require you to further modify the model to imbed some of these probabilities (or their calculations) into the model itself, for the dual purpose of generating samples, and also calculating likelihoods.

That said, I may not be seeing all options clearly here, and hopefully others from the development team can also weigh in, with other ideas and options for you.

messages.body_plain:
A few comments here.

I think the problems are coming from specifying zFirst as "data", then  using zFirst on the right-hand-side:

 z[i,first[i]] <- zFirst[i]

Generally, for initialization of latent z states such as this, what you want is:
A data structure z_data provided in the "data" list, which has 1's for each z[i,t] up to and including the time t of the final positive sighting of each individual, and NA's thereafter
Another data stricture, z_inits, provided in the "inits" list, which has NA's everywhere that z_data has 1's, and then valid initial values thereafter (perhaps, for example, all 1's thereafter.  Or, alternatively, all 0's.  Or, within each row, some number of 1's, followed exclusively by 0's).

That said, without your actual data and not building your model, it's hard to say for sure.

Another comment, with the large - and very sparse - matrices floating around, not to mention all the matrix multiplications taking place, then I have to feel that the model could be hugely sped up with a little more custom math going on.  Tayloring the model code more specifically to only do the calculations that actually use the non-zero matrix values, and not constructing the large matrices in the first place.  This would take a little careful thinking and coding.  But if efficiency ends up being a problem, or perhaps even prohibitive, then you certainly might think about it.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Dear Daniel,
Thanks for you help. I actually found a bug in the matrices, but I would have two questions more about your comments:

- I think the problems are coming from specifying zFirst as "data", then  using zFirst on the right-hand-side:

 z[i,first[i]] <- zFirst[i]

"zFirst" are values for (known) individual state at first encounter. I have fond this in the NIMBLE User Manual: "Values for nodes that appear only on the right-hand side of BUGS declarations (e.g., covariates/predictors) can be provided as constants or as data or initial values. There is no real difference between providing as data or initial values and the values can be added after building a model via setInits or setData." Should I add them *after* nimbleModel()?

- Another comment, with the large - and very sparse - matrices floating around, not to mention all the matrix multiplications taking place, then I have to feel that the model could be hugely sped up with a little more custom math going on.  Tayloring the model code more specifically to only do the calculations that actually use the non-zero matrix values, and not constructing the large matrices in the first place.  This would take a little careful thinking and coding.  But if efficiency ends up being a problem, or perhaps even prohibitive, then you certainly might think about it.

Wonderful. Could you kindly suggest me some examples or material for improving the code?

Thanks,
Simone

On Tuesday, 2 March 2021 at 17:21:58 UTC+1 db...@williams.edu wrote:
> A few comments here.
>
> I think the problems are coming from specifying zFirst as "data", then  using zFirst on the right-hand-side:
>  z[i,first[i]] <- zFirst[i]
>
> Generally, for initialization of latent z states such as this, what you want is:
> A data structure z_data provided in the "data" list, which has 1's for each z[i,t] up to and including the time t of the final positive sighting of each individual, and NA's thereafter
> Another data stricture, z_inits, provided in the "inits" list, which has NA's everywhere that z_data has 1's, and then valid initial values thereafter (perhaps, for example, all 1's thereafter.  Or, alternatively, all 0's.  Or, within each row, some number of 1's, followed exclusively by 0's).
>
> That said, without your actual data and not building your model, it's hard to say for sure.
>
> Another comment, with the large - and very sparse - matrices floating around, not to mention all the matrix multiplications taking place, then I have to feel that the model could be hugely sped up with a little more custom math going on.  Tayloring the model code more specifically to only do the calculations that actually use the non-zero matrix values, and not constructing the large matrices in the first place.  This would take a little careful thinking and coding.  But if efficiency ends up being a problem, or perhaps even prohibitive, then you certainly might think about it.
>
> Daniel

Thanks, Daniel. Already very helpful. I was mostly wondering if I overlooked an easy way to integrate this in nimble. The postprocessing script should be no problem (the only potential problem is that it requires more variables to be monitored).

To follow up on this with a general question: What would be the most convenient way to save and access a variable in a user-defined distribution (or sampler), assuming I want this done potentially with every iteration of the mcmc as with my forward-/backward-probabilities in the hmm?

Am Di., 2. März 2021 um 15:34 Uhr schrieb Daniel Turek <db...@williams.edu>:
> Short answer, Patrick: no, these quantities (samples of the intermediate latent states) are never themselves generated in the calculations done by the nimbleEcology distributions.  The latent states are marginalized over, by propagating a time-sequence of probabilities of each latent state value (at each time period), which are used to calculate the marginal probability of each data observation.
>
> Given what you've said, I think your options are:
> - Not use nimbleEcology, and write the latent states into your model, and thereby have samples of them.
> - Write a post-processing script, as you mentioned, to generate the desired samples using the posterior samples of the model parameters.
> - Modify one of the distributions in nimbleEcology, to use the intermediate probability values to also generate latent states.  Although, from the mechanics of how distributions work in NIMBLE, this would be somewhat awkward, and would (I believe) require you to further modify the model to imbed some of these probabilities (or their calculations) into the model itself, for the dual purpose of generating samples, and also calculating likelihoods.
>
> That said, I may not be seeing all options clearly here, and hopefully others from the development team can also weigh in, with other ideas and options for you.
>
>
> On Tue, Mar 2, 2021 at 9:02 AM Patrick Schmidt <psch...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi everybody,
> >
> > I am playing around with hmm with continuous signals/observations. I implemented a hmm distribution like in the nimbleEcology package. Now I would like to sample from the hidden states (with the forward-backward algorithm).
> >
> > My understading is that this is not implemented in the nimbleEcology package.
> >
> > Any chance I can get intermediate values from the sampling process saved somehow (as in the "generated quantities" option of stan)? Or do I have to write a postprocessing script based on the posterior samples of the high-level parameters and implement this outside of the sampling?
> >
> > Best,
> > Patrick
> >

This is true, everything that's stated in the User Manual.  Nodes that appear only on the RHS (zFirst, here) can be data, or inits, and it won't make a difference if it's data or initial values.  That said, I'm still not sure exactly what's happening with zFirst, and I do feel the observed values of z[,] could be provided as data to the model, again that would be done as:

dataList <- list(...., z = zData)
nimbleModel(...., data = dataList)

where zData is the same size & dimension as z, and contains NA's everywhere, except in the observed locations of z[,], where zData would contain the observed value.

Also, as for avoiding the large matrices, for example, I see that the po[] matrix is constructed as the matrix product of two other (somewhat) large matrics, po1 and po2.  These are fairly sparse.  I would instead suggest constructing the po matrix element-by-element, with most of the elements being zero, and the non-zero elements, defined as:
po[i, j] <- [some expression here involving p, deltaPB, and deltaNB]

This would avoid construction of po1 and po2, and would save a huge number of un-necessary calculations.

Similar could be done with ps[], which is the product of 5 large matrices, so it would really benefit the code to remove all thost multiplications, in a similar way to as I suggested for po[].  I hope this helps.  It will be a little bit of coding, but I believe would speed things up quite a lot.

Hope this helps,
Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Great.  Now, you last question, user-defined distributions cannot and do not have "state" variables which can be set, and accessed later.  Samplers, on the other hand, can maintain state variables, which persist between sampling iteration.  So your best bet might be writing a custom sampler, adding it into the MCMC using
mcmcConfigurationObject$addSampler(type = 'my_custom_sampler', ...)

and having this custom sampler maintain intermediate state variables (as necessary), and it could also access other nodes in the model, perform probability calculations, and even generate samples for latent states (using these probabilities, etc), and store them into a node(s) inside the model.  As for generating these samples during the course of the MCMC, this might be your best bet forward.  Otherwise, the post-processing script, as you've mentioned.

Cheers,
Daniel

On Wed, Mar 3, 2021 at 3:00 AM Patrick Schmidt <psch...@gmail.com> wrote:
> Thanks, Daniel. Already very helpful. I was mostly wondering if I overlooked an easy way to integrate this in nimble. The postprocessing script should be no problem (the only potential problem is that it requires more variables to be monitored).
>
> To follow up on this with a general question: What would be the most convenient way to save and access a variable in a user-defined distribution (or sampler), assuming I want this done potentially with every iteration of the mcmc as with my forward-/backward-probabilities in the hmm?
>
> Am Di., 2. März 2021 um 15:34 Uhr schrieb Daniel Turek <db...@williams.edu>:
> > Short answer, Patrick: no, these quantities (samples of the intermediate latent states) are never themselves generated in the calculations done by the nimbleEcology distributions.  The latent states are marginalized over, by propagating a time-sequence of probabilities of each latent state value (at each time period), which are used to calculate the marginal probability of each data observation.
> >
> > Given what you've said, I think your options are:
> > - Not use nimbleEcology, and write the latent states into your model, and thereby have samples of them.
> > - Write a post-processing script, as you mentioned, to generate the desired samples using the posterior samples of the model parameters.
> > - Modify one of the distributions in nimbleEcology, to use the intermediate probability values to also generate latent states.  Although, from the mechanics of how distributions work in NIMBLE, this would be somewhat awkward, and would (I believe) require you to further modify the model to imbed some of these probabilities (or their calculations) into the model itself, for the dual purpose of generating samples, and also calculating likelihoods.
> >
> > That said, I may not be seeing all options clearly here, and hopefully others from the development team can also weigh in, with other ideas and options for you.
> >
> >
> > On Tue, Mar 2, 2021 at 9:02 AM Patrick Schmidt <psch...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > > Hi everybody,
> > >
> > > I am playing around with hmm with continuous signals/observations. I implemented a hmm distribution like in the nimbleEcology package. Now I would like to sample from the hidden states (with the forward-backward algorithm).
> > >
> > > My understading is that this is not implemented in the nimbleEcology package.
> > >
> > > Any chance I can get intermediate values from the sampling process saved somehow (as in the "generated quantities" option of stan)? Or do I have to write a postprocessing script based on the posterior samples of the high-level parameters and implement this outside of the sampling?
> > >
> > > Best,
> > > Patrick

Hi Everyone,

I fit a lot of hidden Markov like models in Nimble and was wondering if anyone knows an efficient way to sample the parameters that are state dependent. A simple example would be,

y_t ~ Poisson(exp(b0+b1*x_t*S_t)),

where y_t is the dependent count variable, b0 and b1 are parameters, x_t is some covariate and S_t is an unknown binary variable taking the values 0 or 1. S_t might follow a hidden Markov chain (like in a hidden Markov model) or be independent between observations (like a finite mixture model).

Either way, y_t is only a dependency of b1 when S_t=1. That is, when updating b1 the entire loglikelihood does not need to be calculated and this may result in a lot of wasted computational time, especially in large problems.

I was thinking about the best way to deal with this. I came across the RW_llFunction sampler which seems like a good possibility. Although, in large problems with many  state dependent parameters it might become cumbersome. So, I was wondering if I missed something and if there is a better or simpler way to deal with this.

Thanks!

messages.subject_clean: How to extract current iteration
messages.body_plain:
This should be a simple question, I think. How can we extract the current iteration number inside a user-defined sampler?

I want to implement a user-defined sampler ever X iterations. I want to do this because the default sampler does not allow the posterior to be fully explored for this particular model. I have an alternative sampler that does not have this problem, but it is much more computationally costly. However, I only need to use it every once in a while to make sure all disjunct areas of the posterior are sampled. My plan is to recreate both the Nimble default update and the second update inside a user-defined sampler and only use the second one every X iterations. To do this, I need to know which iteration we are currently on.

Thanks,

Ben Augustine

messages.subject_clean: How to extract current iteration
messages.body_plain:
Easiest way:

In the setup code of your sampler function, include:
iterationNumber <- 0

In the run function of your sampler, include:
iterationNumber <<- iterationNumber + 1    ## note the double-assignment arrow, which is necessary
if(iterationNumber %% [how often you want this sampler to operate, e.g. 100 for every 100 MCMC iterations] == 0) {
   ## code for your custom (computationally expensive) sampling algorithm
}

In the reset methods of your sampler, include:
methods = list(
   reset = function() {
      iterationNumber <<- 0
      ## plus anything else you need to reset to a base state, here
   }
)

That should do the trick.

Hi Dirk,

This is a good question.  What we've done in nimbleSCR is to use custom distribution functions that, as a separate argument, take the binary variable as an input.  If that input is 0, the answer is known without more computation and can be returned directly.

It would look like

y_t ~ indicator_Poisson(exp(b0+b1*x_t*S_t), S_t). # S_t can be in both places

In the nimbleSCR case, the calculations inside the functions and distributions that use this trick are quite substantial, so the computational saving is important.

Does that make sense in your use case?

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi, I'm trying to simulate <https://r-nimble.org/nimbleExamples/simulation_from_model.html> species relative abundance data generated from a nested sampling scheme:

Plots are sampled at multiple timepoints. In each plot, we have species relative abundance at 3 randomly-located cores, modeled using the Dirichlet distribution. Plots are grouped together into sites. Mean species abundance at each plot is modeled using abundance at the previous timepoint, site/species random effects, a species intercept, and a predictor.

Adding in the predictor is causing trouble: if I set predictor values to 1, the model converges fine, but if predictor values vary, then some stochastic nodes stop being stochastic (chains are flat). I suspect it is an issue with either my log-link function or model initialization, but I've been tinkering for days to no avail, and would appreciate any advice! (simulation code below)

Thank you,
Zoey

library(nimble)
set.seed(1)

nimbleMod <- nimbleCode({
# First timepoint
for(i in 1:n.core.by.date){
y[i,1:N.spp,1] ~ ddirch(plot_mu[i,1:N.spp,1])
for(s in 1:N.spp){
plot_mu[i,s,1] ~ dgamma(0.01, 0.01) # Plot means for first date
# Convert back to relative abundance
plot_rel[i,s,1] <- plot_mu[i,s,1] / sum(plot_mu[i,1:N.spp,1])
}
}
for (t in 2:N.date){
for(i in 1:n.core.by.date){
# Core observations (3 per plot):
y[i,1:N.spp,t] ~ ddirch(plot_mu[i,1:N.spp,t])
# Process model determines plot mean
log(plot_mu[i,1:N.spp,t]) <- intercept[1:N.spp] +
site_effect[siteID[i],1:N.spp] + beta_IC[1:N.spp]*log(plot_mu[i,1:N.spp,t-1]) + beta_mat[1:N.spp]*mat[plotID[i],t]
for(s in 1:N.spp){
plot_rel[i,s,t] <- plot_mu[i,s,t] / sum(plot_mu[i,1:N.spp,t])
}
}
}
# Prior for site effects (zero for the first site):
for(s in 1:N.spp){
site_effect[1,s] <- 0
for(k in 2:N.site){
site_effect[k,s] ~ dnorm(0, 10)
}
}
# Prior for intercepts (zero for the first species):
intercept[1] <- 0
beta_IC[1] <- 0
beta_mat[1] <- 0
for(s in 2:N.spp){
intercept[s] ~ dnorm(0, 10)
beta_IC[s] ~ dnorm(0, 10)
beta_mat[s] ~ dnorm(0, 10)
}
}) #end NIMBLE model.

constants <- list(N.site = 4,
N.plot =  20,
N.spp = 3,
n.core.by.date = 60,
N.date = 6,
siteID = rep(c(1:4), each = 15),
plotID = rep(c(1:20), each = 3))
# This does not work (chains become flat)
#mat <- matrix(rnorm(constants$N.plot * constants$N.date, 0, .5),
# nrow = constants$N.plot, ncol = constants$N.date)
# This works
mat <- matrix(rep(1, constants$N.plot * constants$N.date),
nrow = constants$N.plot, ncol = constants$N.date)
constants$mat = mat

# Assumes 3 cores per plot
initsFun <- function(constants){
core_per_plot <- 3
y_init <- array(rep(DirichletReg::rdirichlet(constants$N.plot * core_per_plot,
rep(2, constants$N.spp)), constants$N.date),
dim = c(constants$N.plot * core_per_plot, constants$N.spp, constants$N.date))
site_eff_init <- matrix(rnorm(constants$N.site * constants$N.spp,
0,1),
nrow = constants$N.site,
ncol = constants$N.spp)
site_eff_init[1] <- 0
plot_mu_init <- array(rnorm(constants$N.plot * core_per_plot * constants$N.spp * constants$N.date,
2,.2),
dim = c(constants$N.plot * core_per_plot, constants$N.spp, constants$N.date))
intercept_init <- rnorm(constants$N.spp,1,1)
intercept_init[1] <- 0
beta_IC_init <- rnorm(constants$N.spp,1,1)
beta_IC_init[1] <- 0
beta_mat_init <- rnorm(constants$N.spp,1,.1)
beta_mat_init[1] <- 0
return(list(
y = y_init,
intercept = intercept_init,
site_effect = site_eff_init,
plot_mu = plot_mu_init,
beta_IC = beta_IC_init,
beta_mat = beta_mat_init))
}

## Configure and run model
Rmodel <- nimbleModel(code = nimbleMod,
constants = constants,
inits = initsFun(constants))

# Simulate data and add it to the model
nodesToSim <- Rmodel$getDependencies(c("plot_mu"), self = F, downstream = T)
Rmodel$simulate(nodesToSim)
simulatedYs <- Rmodel$y
head(simulatedYs)
tail(simulatedYs)
Rmodel$setData(list(y = simulatedYs))

# Compile model
CsimModel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)

# Configure & compile MCMC
mcmcConf <- configureMCMC(CsimModel)
mcmcConf$addMonitors("plot_mu","plot_rel","y","site_mu","beta_IC","beta_mat","intercept")
simMCMC <- buildMCMC(mcmcConf)
compiled <- compileNimble(simMCMC, project = CsimModel, resetFunctions = T)

# Sample from MCMC
samples <- runMCMC(compiled, niter = 1000, nburnin = 500,
nchains = 3, samplesAsCodaMCMC = T, thin = 3)

Thanks Perry!

I think this will help, but maybe not completely solve the problem unless I am missing something. Do you mean,

 indicator_Poisson(exp(b0+b1*x_t*S_t), S_t) =    Poisson(exp(b0+b1*x_t*S_t)) if S_t=1
                                                                                     Poisson(exp(b0)) if S_t=0 ?

In that case when sampling b1 it would calculate exp(b0) for all y_t where S_t=0, which is still unnecessary. It is better then calculating exp(b0+b1*x_t*S_t) for all y_t where S_t=0, but it would be better to not calculate any y_t where S_t=0 as it would drop from the MH ratio anyway.

messages.body_plain:
I'll keep this very brief, since I have to.  But I've been thinking about this for a while, since Dirk's first email.  It's not an immediately easy question, and I agree with Dirk that the prospect of just using a custom distribution in place of dpois wouldn't do the trick.  I came up with one option, using nimbleFunction lists, which I think would work, but would require somewhat substantial extra coding.  The other idea I came up with - but may or may not be useful, depending on how similar your example code is to your actual model - is to hard-code the data-likelihood (in this case, the dpois for y[t]) into the llFunction specialized nimbleFunction, and using the RW_llFunction sampler as Dirk initially thought.  In that custom-written llFunction, it would element-by-element inspect S[t], and either calculate, or not calculate, the likelihood of each y[t].  This would work, but it's generality could be limited by other aspects of the model, if other sampled dimensions also depend on any y[t].  But it's one idea.  I've also been trying to think from an angle of combinations of a custom likelihood and a custom sampler, which maybe could work, but I don't see the full picture as of yet.  I hope this helps a little, and we can figure something out for you, Dirk.  Let us know if you think the idea mentioned above might work, or not.

Daniel

messages.body_plain:
Thanks for looking into it Daniel.

" In that custom-written llFunction, it would element-by-element inspect S[t], and either calculate, or not calculate, the likelihood of each y[t]."

I think that is the way to go. Broadly, the issue is that Nimble does not partition the likelihood efficiently for mixture like models. I will give a more general example. Consider a general case where S_t is in 1,...,m and p(y_t|S_t=k,theta)=p(y_t|S_t=k,theta_k) for k=1,...,m, where theta=(theta_1,....,theta_m). The likelihood conditional on (S_1,...,S_T) is,

p(y_1,....,y_T|S_1,....,S_T) = prod[t=1 to T] p(y_t|S_t,theta).

This is what Nimble would use to update any elements of theta and it would calculate the entire thing. But the likelihood can be partitioned as,

p(y_1,....,y_T|S_1,....,S_T) = prod[t such that S_t=1] p(y_t|S_t=1,theta_1) *....*  prod[t such that S_t=m] p(y_t|S_t=m,theta_m) .

So, in updating theta_k only prod[t such that S_t=k] p(y_t|S_t=k,theta_k), needs to be calculated. With the RW_llFunction sampler the user should be able to just supply "prod[t such that S_t=k] p(y_t|S_t=k,theta_k)" as the likelihood in sampling theta_k. The only issue is you would have to write it for k=1,...,m and it is a little cumbersome.

messages.subject: Re: Best way to sample a parameter whose dependencies depend on another sampled parameter?
messages.subject_clean: Best way to sample a parameter whose dependencies depend on another sampled parameter?
messages.body_plain:
Yes, I agree there is this potential inefficiency.  When we implemented stochastic indexing, we thought about ways to be clever like this, but they go too complicated too quickly.

I like the idea of combining a user-defined distribution with a custom sampler that makes the calculations efficiently.  Isn't this similar to what is built into nimble for CAR distributions and samplers?  It's a question of where to put calculations that are done at least somewhat outside of the model, either in a custom likelihood with RW_llFunction or in a custom sampler.  In a custom sampler, I think there could be a somewhat generic setup that knows what the nodes corresponding to S_t values are and their corresponding dependencies (y_t) and only calculates the ones needed for a candidate value of k.

For the record, my original answer was hasty and made a hash of it.  I was thinking you could use the indicator (binary) variable to interrupt calculations at whatever step is needed, possibly multiple steps, which wasn't shown clearly.  But the problem you're stating is more general and different.

OTOH, maybe this answer is hasty too!

Perry

On Thu, Mar 4, 2021 at 3:41 PM dirkdouw...@gmail.com <dirkdouw...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Thanks for looking into it Daniel.
>
> " In that custom-written llFunction, it would element-by-element inspect S[t], and either calculate, or not calculate, the likelihood of each y[t]."
>
> I think that is the way to go. Broadly, the issue is that Nimble does not partition the likelihood efficiently for mixture like models. I will give a more general example. Consider a general case where S_t is in 1,...,m and p(y_t|S_t=k,theta)=p(y_t|S_t=k,theta_k) for k=1,...,m, where theta=(theta_1,....,theta_m). The likelihood conditional on (S_1,...,S_T) is,
>
> p(y_1,....,y_T|S_1,....,S_T) = prod[t=1 to T] p(y_t|S_t,theta).
>
> This is what Nimble would use to update any elements of theta and it would calculate the entire thing. But the likelihood can be partitioned as,
>
> p(y_1,....,y_T|S_1,....,S_T) = prod[t such that S_t=1] p(y_t|S_t=1,theta_1) *....*  prod[t such that S_t=m] p(y_t|S_t=m,theta_m) .
>
> So, in updating theta_k only prod[t such that S_t=k] p(y_t|S_t=k,theta_k), needs to be calculated. With the RW_llFunction sampler the user should be able to just supply "prod[t such that S_t=k] p(y_t|S_t=k,theta_k)" as the likelihood in sampling theta_k. The only issue is you would have to write it for k=1,...,m and it is a little cumbersome.
>
>
>

It's not an immediately easy question, and I agree with Dirk that the prospect of just using a custom distribution in place of dpois wouldn't do the trick.  I came up with one option, using nimbleFunction lists, which I think would work, but would require somewhat substantial extra coding.  The other idea I came up with - but may or may not be useful, depending on how similar your example code is to your actual model - is to hard-code the data-likelihood (in this case, the dpois for y[t]) into the llFunction specialized nimbleFunction, and using the RW_llFunction sampler as Dirk initially thought.  In that custom-written llFunction, it would element-by-element inspect S[t], and either calculate, or not calculate, the likelihood of each y[t].  This would work, but it's generality could be limited by other aspects of the model, if other sampled dimensions also depend on any y[t].  But it's one idea.  I've also been trying to think from an angle of combinations of a custom likelihood and a custom sampler, which maybe could work, but I don't see the full picture as of yet.  I hope this helps a little, and we can figure something out for you, Dirk.  Let us know if you think the idea mentioned above might work, or not.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Zoey,

I ran your code and I see the monitored elements that are not moving, but it's not clear to me that anything is wrong.

1) beta_IC[1], int[1], beta_mat[1], site_effect[1, 1:3] don't move, but all of these are fixed in the model, so they shouldn't move.

2) The components of plot_mu[1:60, 1:3, 1] are all moving, as they should since they are stochastic elements in the model.

3) The remaining elements of plot_mu are all deterministic so whether they move depends on whether the stochastic elements that they depend on move.
All of the ones that don't move seem to correspond to species #1, (i.e., plot_mu[1:60, 1, 1:6]) and they shouldn't move because they are fixed because of point #1 above -
namely they are determined by the fact that beta_IC[1]=0, int[1]=0, etc.

I might be missing something. If so, please let me know specifically which of the elements you think should not be constant over the course of the MCMC.

-chris

On Thu, Mar 4, 2021 at 1:32 PM Zoey Werbin <zoeyw...@gmail.com> wrote:

> Hi, I'm trying to simulate <https://r-nimble.org/nimbleExamples/simulation_from_model.html> species relative abundance data generated from a nested sampling scheme:
>
> Plots are sampled at multiple timepoints. In each plot, we have species relative abundance at 3 randomly-located cores, modeled using the Dirichlet distribution. Plots are grouped together into sites. Mean species abundance at each plot is modeled using abundance at the previous timepoint, site/species random effects, a species intercept, and a predictor.
>
> Adding in the predictor is causing trouble: if I set predictor values to 1, the model converges fine, but if predictor values vary, then some stochastic nodes stop being stochastic (chains are flat). I suspect it is an issue with either my log-link function or model initialization, but I've been tinkering for days to no avail, and would appreciate any advice! (simulation code below)
>
> Thank you,
> Zoey
>
> library(nimble)
> set.seed(1)
>
> nimbleMod <- nimbleCode({
> # First timepoint
> for(i in 1:n.core.by.date){
> y[i,1:N.spp,1] ~ ddirch(plot_mu[i,1:N.spp,1])
> for(s in 1:N.spp){
> plot_mu[i,s,1] ~ dgamma(0.01, 0.01) # Plot means for first date
> # Convert back to relative abundance
> plot_rel[i,s,1] <- plot_mu[i,s,1] / sum(plot_mu[i,1:N.spp,1])
> }
> }
> for (t in 2:N.date){
> for(i in 1:n.core.by.date){
> # Core observations (3 per plot):
> y[i,1:N.spp,t] ~ ddirch(plot_mu[i,1:N.spp,t])
> # Process model determines plot mean
> log(plot_mu[i,1:N.spp,t]) <- intercept[1:N.spp] +
> site_effect[siteID[i],1:N.spp] + beta_IC[1:N.spp]*log(plot_mu[i,1:N.spp,t-1]) + beta_mat[1:N.spp]*mat[plotID[i],t]
> for(s in 1:N.spp){
> plot_rel[i,s,t] <- plot_mu[i,s,t] / sum(plot_mu[i,1:N.spp,t])
> }
> }
> }
> # Prior for site effects (zero for the first site):
> for(s in 1:N.spp){
> site_effect[1,s] <- 0
> for(k in 2:N.site){
> site_effect[k,s] ~ dnorm(0, 10)
> }
> }
> # Prior for intercepts (zero for the first species):
> intercept[1] <- 0
> beta_IC[1] <- 0
> beta_mat[1] <- 0
> for(s in 2:N.spp){
> intercept[s] ~ dnorm(0, 10)
> beta_IC[s] ~ dnorm(0, 10)
> beta_mat[s] ~ dnorm(0, 10)
> }
> }) #end NIMBLE model.
>
> constants <- list(N.site = 4,
> N.plot =  20,
> N.spp = 3,
> n.core.by.date = 60,
> N.date = 6,
> siteID = rep(c(1:4), each = 15),
> plotID = rep(c(1:20), each = 3))
> # This does not work (chains become flat)
> #mat <- matrix(rnorm(constants$N.plot * constants$N.date, 0, .5),
> # nrow = constants$N.plot, ncol = constants$N.date)
> # This works
> mat <- matrix(rep(1, constants$N.plot * constants$N.date),
> nrow = constants$N.plot, ncol = constants$N.date)
> constants$mat = mat
>
> # Assumes 3 cores per plot
> initsFun <- function(constants){
> core_per_plot <- 3
> y_init <- array(rep(DirichletReg::rdirichlet(constants$N.plot * core_per_plot,
> rep(2, constants$N.spp)), constants$N.date),
> dim = c(constants$N.plot * core_per_plot, constants$N.spp, constants$N.date))
> site_eff_init <- matrix(rnorm(constants$N.site * constants$N.spp,
> 0,1),
> nrow = constants$N.site,
> ncol = constants$N.spp)
> site_eff_init[1] <- 0
> plot_mu_init <- array(rnorm(constants$N.plot * core_per_plot * constants$N.spp * constants$N.date,
> 2,.2),
> dim = c(constants$N.plot * core_per_plot, constants$N.spp, constants$N.date))
> intercept_init <- rnorm(constants$N.spp,1,1)
> intercept_init[1] <- 0
> beta_IC_init <- rnorm(constants$N.spp,1,1)
> beta_IC_init[1] <- 0
> beta_mat_init <- rnorm(constants$N.spp,1,.1)
> beta_mat_init[1] <- 0
> return(list(
> y = y_init,
> intercept = intercept_init,
> site_effect = site_eff_init,
> plot_mu = plot_mu_init,
> beta_IC = beta_IC_init,
> beta_mat = beta_mat_init))
> }
>
> ## Configure and run model
> Rmodel <- nimbleModel(code = nimbleMod,
> constants = constants,
> inits = initsFun(constants))
>
> # Simulate data and add it to the model
> nodesToSim <- Rmodel$getDependencies(c("plot_mu"), self = F, downstream = T)
> Rmodel$simulate(nodesToSim)
> simulatedYs <- Rmodel$y
> head(simulatedYs)
> tail(simulatedYs)
> Rmodel$setData(list(y = simulatedYs))
>
> # Compile model
> CsimModel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)
>
> # Configure & compile MCMC
> mcmcConf <- configureMCMC(CsimModel)
> mcmcConf$addMonitors("plot_mu","plot_rel","y","site_mu","beta_IC","beta_mat","intercept")
> simMCMC <- buildMCMC(mcmcConf)
> compiled <- compileNimble(simMCMC, project = CsimModel, resetFunctions = T)
>
> # Sample from MCMC
> samples <- runMCMC(compiled, niter = 1000, nburnin = 500,
> nchains = 3, samplesAsCodaMCMC = T, thin = 3)
>

Dirk, that's a fair concern about writing these functions, I believe you mean the repeated specific llFunction's, one for each value 1....m. Happy to discuss this further, if it's helpful.

Daniel

It's not an immediately easy question, and I agree with Dirk that the prospect of just using a custom distribution in place of dpois wouldn't do the trick.  I came up with one option, using nimbleFunction lists, which I think would work, but would require somewhat substantial extra coding.  The other idea I came up with - but may or may not be useful, depending on how similar your example code is to your actual model - is to hard-code the data-likelihood (in this case, the dpois for y[t]) into the llFunction specialized nimbleFunction, and using the RW_llFunction sampler as Dirk initially thought.  In that custom-written llFunction, it would element-by-element inspect S[t], and either calculate, or not calculate, the likelihood of each y[t].  This would work, but it's generality could be limited by other aspects of the model, if other sampled dimensions also depend on any y[t].  But it's one idea.  I've also been trying to think from an angle of combinations of a custom likelihood and a custom sampler, which maybe could work, but I don't see the full picture as of yet.  I hope this helps a little, and we can figure something out for you, Dirk.  Let us know if you think the idea mentioned above might work, or not.

Kind regards,
Oana Petrof

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,

Thanks for your reply. I reformulated the model code to make most of the deterministic effects random, but now I'm getting errors relating to model initialization ("warning: problem initializing stochastic node y[1, 1:3, 4]: logProb less than -1e12," and logProb is Inf for some nodes) even though I've provided a list with initial values for y and plot_mu. Is there something fundamental I'm missing with respect to how values are initialized?

Below is the newer code (you can see where I started testing how model can estimate NA data nodes, but I didn't get to that because of the errors). Thanks again for any pointers.

nimbleMod <- nimbleCode({
# First timepoint
for(i in 1:n.core.by.date){
y[i,1:N.spp,1] ~ ddirch(plot_mu[i,1:N.spp,1])
for(s in 1:N.spp){
plot_mu[i,s,1] ~ dgamma(0.01, 0.01) # Plot means for first date
# Convert back to relative abundance
plot_rel[i,s,1] <- plot_mu[i,s,1] / sum(plot_mu[i,1:N.spp,1])
}
}
for (t in 2:N.date){
for(i in 1:n.core.by.date){
# Core observations (3 per plot):
y[i,1:N.spp,t] ~ ddirch(plot_mu[i,1:N.spp,t])
# Process model determines plot mean

log(plot_mu[i,1:N.spp,t]) <- beta_IC[1:N.spp]*log(plot_mu[i,1:N.spp,t-1]) + # Previous timepoint
beta_mat[1:N.spp]*mat[plotID[i],t] + # Environmental predictor
beta_int[1:N.spp]*int[plotID[i]] + # Intercept
site_effect[siteID[i],1:N.spp] # Site random effect
for(s in 1:N.spp){

# Convert back to relative abundance

plot_rel[i,s,t] <- plot_mu[i,s,t] / sum(plot_mu[i,1:N.spp,t])
}
}
}

# Priors for site random effects:
for(s in 1:N.spp){
for(k in 1:N.site){
site_effect[k,s] ~ dnorm(0, 3)
}
}
# Priors for fixed effects:
for(s in 1:N.spp){
beta_mat[s] ~ dnorm(0, 3)
beta_IC[s] ~ dnorm(0, 3)
}
# Priors for intercept:
beta_int[1] <- 0
for(s in 2:N.spp){
beta_int[s] ~ dnorm(0, 3)
}

}) #end NIMBLE model.

# Now generate list of constants (no data)

constants <- list(N.site = 4,
N.plot =  20,
N.spp = 3,
n.core.by.date = 60,
N.date = 6,
siteID = rep(c(1:4), each = 15),
plotID = rep(c(1:20), each = 3))

# Add in covariate data
constants$mat <- matrix(rnorm(constants$N.plot * constants$N.date, 0, .5),

  nrow = constants$N.plot, ncol = constants$N.date)

constants$int <- rep(1, constants$N.plot)

# Initialization function

initsFun <- function(constants){
core_per_plot <- 3
y_init <- array(rep(DirichletReg::rdirichlet(constants$N.plot * core_per_plot,
rep(2, constants$N.spp)), constants$N.date),
dim = c(constants$N.plot * core_per_plot, constants$N.spp, constants$N.date))
site_eff_init <- matrix(rnorm(constants$N.site * constants$N.spp,
0,1),
nrow = constants$N.site,
ncol = constants$N.spp)

plot_mu_init <- array(rnorm(constants$N.plot * core_per_plot * constants$N.spp * constants$N.date,
2,.2),
dim = c(constants$N.plot * core_per_plot, constants$N.spp, constants$N.date))
intercept_init <- rnorm(constants$N.spp,1,1)
intercept_init[1] <- 0
beta_IC_init <- rnorm(constants$N.spp,1,1)

beta_mat_init <- rnorm(constants$N.spp,1,.1)
return(list(
y = y_init,

site_effect = site_eff_init,
plot_mu = plot_mu_init,
beta_IC = beta_IC_init,

beta_mat = beta_mat_init,
beta_int = intercept_init))
}

initsList <- initsFun(constants)

## Configure and run model
Rmodel <- nimbleModel(code = nimbleMod,
constants = constants,

inits = initsList)

# Simulate data from model

nodesToSim <- Rmodel$getDependencies(c("plot_mu"), self = F, downstream = T)
Rmodel$simulate(nodesToSim)
simulatedYs <- Rmodel$y
head(simulatedYs)
tail(simulatedYs)

# Now let's add those simulated values to the model, but replacing some values with NA to test estimation of missing data
# simulatedYs[1,,2] <- NA
# simulatedYs[4,,3] <- NA
# simulatedYs[6,,4] <- NA

Rmodel$setData(list(y = simulatedYs))

# Compile model
CsimModel <- compileNimble(Rmodel)

# Configure & compile MCMC
mcmcConf <- configureMCMC(CsimModel)

mcmcConf$addMonitors("plot_mu","plot_rel","y","beta_IC","beta_mat","beta_int")

simMCMC <- buildMCMC(mcmcConf)
compiled <- compileNimble(simMCMC, project = CsimModel, resetFunctions = T)

# Sample from MCMC
samples <- runMCMC(compiled, niter = 1000, nburnin = 500,
nchains = 3, samplesAsCodaMCMC = T, thin = 3)

Hi,

A MWE is provided in the attached ZIP folder (I'm using a Windows 10 OS).

I'm probably doing something dumb, but can't spot it at the moment. I was hoping a fresh set of eyes could get me going in the right direction.

Thanks!

Josh

Hi Josh,

I think the issue you're having is due to two small problems with easy fixes.

First, any data that's used for indexing--in this case, "site" and "year" vectors--needs to be provided in "constants." This will clear that super long warning about dynamic indices.

Second, in your custom NIMBLE function, your arguments look like they need "= double(0)" (scalar) instead of "= double(1)" vector.

Fixing these two should let you compile the model.

Ben

It looks like some of your plot_mu values are getting very large (e.g., 10^15) and this is causing some numerical issues. One thing seems to be that some of the y's get simulated to be exactly zero or one, because
of numerical imprecision and then that may cause some of what you are seeing (though I didn't track through things in detail). So my suggestion is that given plot_mu is the result of exponentiation, be careful about the values
that go into calculating log(plot_mu).

Also, it may not matter, but I'm not following why you initialize plot_mu and y in the inits and then you do Rmodel$simulate() and overwrite them...

messages.body_plain:
Just a note that it looks like plot_mu is excluded from nodesToSim (self = F), and then it makes sense to be simulating from y assuming that's your intention.

Zoey, in case it's not clear, the problem with a numerical 0 or 1 (meaning a value that isn't just very very close to 0 or 1) is the Dirichlet isn't defined for values that are actually 0 or 1, only values between 0 and 1.

In general a strategy to track down where the problem is would be to backtrack through the model starting from the problem node.  It would look like;
Cmodel$y[1, 1:3, 4] # see what's there
Cmodel$plot_mu[1, 1:3, 4] # this is the parameter for y[1, 1:3, 4]
Cmodel$beta_IC[1:3] # next step back, etc.
# If you need to check a specific calculation, e.g.
Cmodel$calculate("y[1, 1:3, 4]")
# Maybe try some new simulations to get a feel for the situation
Cmodel$simulate( Cmodel$getDependencies("plot_mu[1, 1:3, 4]"))
# etc.

HTH!
Perry

messages.body_plain:
Good evening Chris

I expect I am having the same issue with a simple N-mixture model. However, I do not have the ability to remove the location because it is essential to downstream analyses. Are there any other options? I thought the initial values were the problem; however, if I remove the spatial component I do not have the problem. I appreciate any input.

Respectfully,

Anthony Snead

On Thursday, November 12, 2020 at 11:52:43 AM UTC-6 christophe...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi Gary,
>
> (Note to others reading this, this response follows some off-list discussion in which Gary shared his data with me.)
>
> It looks like the issue is that the 50th location has 0 neighbors and also has a 0 count. This means that the inference for phi[50] is unconstrained by the CAR prior (since there are no neighbors) and unconstrained by the data (since the likelihood increases as the mean of the Poisson for the observation at the 50th location goes to zero). So either in the zero_mean=0 or zero_mean=1 case, you will see phi[50] wandering off towards minus infinity. In the zero_mean=1 case the side effect is that the other phi values need to increase to offset phi[50].
>
> I would suggest simply taking that location out of the modeling.
>
> -Chris
>
>
> On Tue, Nov 10, 2020 at 2:20 PM Chris Paciorek <christophe...@gmail.com> wrote:
> > Hi Akis,
> >
> > Can you tell us which values go off to Inf or NaN?  If so, we could help to diagnose what the problem is.
> >
> > I do generally recommend that you remove alpha and let the intercept be the mean of the phi values with zero_mean=0 (as you've read). Is there a reason you can't use the mean of the phi values in place of alpha? It really should be equivalent given you have a flat prior on alpha in your attempt with zero_mean = 1.
> >
> > -chris
> >
> >
> >
> > ---------- Forwarded message ---------
> > From: Konstantinoudis Akis <g.konsta...@gmail.com>
> > Date: Tue, Nov 10, 2020 at 6:48 AM
> > Subject: Inf or NaN in BYM when zero_mean = 1
> > To: nimble-users <nimble...@googlegroups.com>
> >
> >
> > Hi all,
> >
> > I hope I find you well.
> >
> > I have been trying to fit a very simple BYM model in NIMBLE. The code is as follows:
> >
> > BYMCode <- nimbleCode(
> > {
> >   for (i in 1:N){
> >
> >     O[i] ~ dpois(mu[i])                                                         # Poisson likelihood for observed counts
> >     log(mu[i]) <- log(E[i]) + alpha + theta[i] + phi[i]
> >
> >     theta[i] ~ dnorm(0, tau = tau.theta)         # area-specific RE
> >     RR[i] <- exp(alpha + theta[i] + phi[i])                # area-specific RR
> >     resRR[i] <- exp(theta[i] + phi[i])                 # area-specific residual RR
> >     e[i] <- (O[i]-mu[i])/sqrt(mu[i])                                     # residuals
> >     proba.resRR[i]<-step(resRR[i]-1)                                   # Posterior probability
> >   }
> >
> >   # BYM prior
> >   phi[1:N] ~ dcar_normal(adj = adj[1:L], weights = weights[1:L], num = num[1:N], tau = tau.phi)
> >
> >   # Priors
> >   alpha ~ dflat()                                                               # vague prior (Unif(-inf, +inf))
> >   overallRR <- exp(alpha)                                                # overall RR across study region
> >
> >   tau.theta ~ dgamma(0.5, 0.05)                                   # prior for the precision hyperparameter
> >   sigma2.theta <- 1/tau.theta                                          # variance of unstructured area random effects
> >
> >   tau.phi ~ dgamma(0.5, 0.0005)                                    # prior on precison of spatial area random effects
> >   sigma2.phi <- 1/tau.phi                                                    # conditional variance of spatial area random effects
> >   sigma2.phi.marginal <- sd(phi[1:N])*sd(phi[1:N])        # empirical marginal variance of spatial effects
> >
> >   frac.spatial <-  sigma2.phi.marginal/( sigma2.phi.marginal + sigma2.theta)    # fraction of total variation in log RR
> >
> > }
> > )
> >
> > n.LTLA <- dim(COVID19Deaths)[1]
> >
> > # Format the data for NIMBLE in a list
> > COVIDdata = list(
> >                  O = COVID19Deaths$deaths                      # observed nb of deaths
> > )
> >
> > COVIDConsts <-list(
> >                  N = n.LTLA,                                   # nb of LTLAs
> >                  L = length(nbWB_A$weights),                   # the number of neighboring areas
> >                  E = COVID19Deaths$expected,                   # expected number of deaths
> >                  adj = nbWB_A$adj,                             # the elements of the neighbouring matrix
> >                  num = nbWB_A$num,
> >                  weights = nbWB_A$weights
> > )
> >
> > inits <- list(
> >   list(alpha = 0.01,
> >        tau.theta = 10,
> >        tau.phi = 1,
> >        theta = rep(0.01, times = 317),
> >        phi = c(rep(0.5, times = 158), 0, rep(-0.5, times = 158))
> >        ),
> >   list(alpha = 0.5,
> >        tau.theta = 1,
> >        tau.phi = 0.1,
> >        theta = rep(0.05, times = 317),
> >        phi = c(rep(0.05, times = 158), 0, rep(-0.05, times = 158))
> >        )
> > )
> >
> > params <- c("sigma2.theta", "sigma2.phi","overallRR", "RR", "theta",
> >              "resRR", "frac.spatial", "sigma2.phi.marginal", "proba.resRR", "mu")
> >
> >
> > ni <- 50000  #nb iterations
> > nt <- 5     #thinning interval
> > nb <- 10000  #nb iterations as burning
> > nc <- 2     #nb chains
> >
> > t0<- Sys.time()
> > modelBYM.sim <- nimbleMCMC(code = BYMCode,
> >                       data = COVIDdata,
> >                       constants = COVIDConsts,
> >                       inits = inits,
> >                       monitors = params,
> >                       niter = ni,
> >                       nburnin = nb,
> >                       thin = nt,
> >                       nchains = nc,
> >                       setSeed = 9,
> >                       progressBar = TRUE,
> >                       samplesAsCodaMCMC = TRUE,
> >                       summary = TRUE,
> >                       WAIC = TRUE
> >                       )
> > t1<- Sys.time()
> > t1 - t0
> >
> >
> >
> > So the model runs smoothly if you exclude the phi (ie the ICAR component). I have tried several things, but imposing sum to zero constraints is important because the intercept is smth I need to have. I have tried several things:
> >
> > 1. If I remove the zero_mean = 1, it works but it never converges, I have tried a lot of different niter. I have read that it could be better if I remove the intercept under the zero_mean specification, but I want to keep the intercept.
> >
> > 2. I have played with the priors of the hyperparameters and intercept.
> >
> > 3. Notice that I imposed also the contraints as we used to do in winbugs (making the initial values to sum to zero) but this didnt work too
> >
> > any ideas?
> >
> > Best wishes,
> > Gary
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >
> >

messages.subject: Re: Inf or NaN in BYM when zero_mean = 1
messages.subject_clean: Inf or NaN in BYM when zero_mean = 1
messages.body_plain:
hi Anthony,

If a location has no neighbors, then there is no information coming from the spatial structure. So then one is relying solely on the data, and if the count is zero, the likelihood says that the best value for the mean of the Poisson is a value that is as infinitesimally close to zero. So that's not so helpful. So in principle one would need to either have a somewhat informative prior for the mean of the Poisson for that location or just give up and decide to fix the mean of that Poisson at some plausible value.

All that being said, I'm not fully understanding why removing the spatial component would solve the problem. What is your prior on the mean of the Poisson for that location when you remove the spatial component? I suppose if you set a prior that amounts to having a somewhat informative prior, then what you are seeing is consistent with my analysis above.

-chris

> > It looks like the issue is that the 50th location has 0 neighbors and also has a 0 count. This means that the inference for phi[50] is unconstrained by the CAR prior (since there are no neighbors) and unconstrained by the data (since the likelihood increases as the mean of the Poisson for the observation at the 50th location goes to zero). So either in the zero_mean=0 or zero_mean=1 case, you will see phi[50] wandering off towards minus infinity. In the zero_mean=1 case the side effect is that the other phi values need to increase to offset phi[50].
> >

messages.subject: Re: how to aggregate predictions from hiarchiarchial model within nimble code
messages.subject_clean: how to aggregate predictions from hiarchiarchial model within nimble code
messages.body_plain:
Hi Cam,

Thanks for the question.  I think there are a couple of issues and ways to approach this.

I am not sure, but your code as written looks imperative (typical programming), but the model language is declarative.  What that means is you can't re-use the same elements of x in the innermost 2 loops.  I am not sure why you got exactly that error message and would need to see a more complete (including call to nimbleModel) or fully reproducible example to track that down, but a good starting point is avoiding re-use of x.

Here is a way you could do it without the income and education loops, so p_pop is declared at the innermost of the first four loops:

p_pop[count_index[i_zip, i_age, i_eth, i_male]] <- average_over_income_edu(b[1] + b[2] * (i_male-1) +  b[3] * x_zip_hisp[i_zip] +  a_zip[i_zip] + a_eth[i_eth] + a_age[i_age], a_income[1:6], a_edu[1:2])

where outside of the model you write:

average_over_income_edu <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function( other_terms = double(), a_income = double(1), a_edu = double(1)) {
  ans <- 0
for(i in 1:length(a_income)) {
  for(j in 1:length(a_edu)) {
   ans <- ans + expit(other_terms + a_income[i] + a_edu[j])
  }
}
ans <-, ans / (length(a_income) * length(a_edu))
return(ans)
returnType(double())
}

What this is doing is moving the non-declarative processing you need outside of the model.

Another option to mention is that there is a second set of monitors, with their own thinning interval, available in the MCMC.  You can set monitors2 to the predictions you need and use a larger thinning interval (thin2) than you might want for the main model parameters.  That way you'd get a smaller data structure.

I hope that helps.  Let us know more questions.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Enrico,

First, I'll point out that in general you can end up with vectors that are zero length and with loops that loop over nothing because it is possible for t1final, t2final, etc. to be zero.
When you try to create a vector 1:0, nimble will just treat that as a zero-length vector and if you have a loop like "for(i in 1:0)" , nimble won't run the loop.

However, consider the following code:

for (i in 1:t2final) {n2[i] = (n1[t1final])  * (1+r2)^t2[i]}

If one has t2final > 0 and t1final = 0, that causes the seg fault because there is an attempt to access a location in memory that is invalid (namely n1[0], which is actually translated to n1[-1] in C++).

So you need to add some code that deals with such cases where the changepoints are so close to each other (or to the ends of the full interval) that the rounding causes them to be equal.

A few other side notes of things I noticed when looking at your code:
1) you shouldn't need chp1, chp2, etc. Just pass chp[1], chp[2] directly into your function call
2) why do you use abs()?  You know that a >= mu1, mu1 >= mu2, etc. so you could just do "a-mu1", etc.
3) You use round() both in the nimble model code and in the function.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Chris,
That makes sense - thanks! Worked using the following prior:

  chp1 ~ dunif(b,a);
  chp2 ~ T(dunif(b,a),b,round(chp1))
  chp3 ~ T(dunif(b,a),b,round(chp2))

All Best,
Enrico

On Friday, 12 March 2021 at 02:43:58 UTC christophe...@gmail.com wrote:
> Hi Enrico,
>
> First, I'll point out that in general you can end up with vectors that are zero length and with loops that loop over nothing because it is possible for t1final, t2final, etc. to be zero.
> When you try to create a vector 1:0, nimble will just treat that as a zero-length vector and if you have a loop like "for(i in 1:0)" , nimble won't run the loop.
>
> However, consider the following code:
>
> for (i in 1:t2final) {n2[i] = (n1[t1final])  * (1+r2)^t2[i]}
>
> If one has t2final > 0 and t1final = 0, that causes the seg fault because there is an attempt to access a location in memory that is invalid (namely n1[0], which is actually translated to n1[-1] in C++).
>
> So you need to add some code that deals with such cases where the changepoints are so close to each other (or to the ends of the full interval) that the rounding causes them to be equal.
>
> A few other side notes of things I noticed when looking at your code:
> 1) you shouldn't need chp1, chp2, etc. Just pass chp[1], chp[2] directly into your function call
> 2) why do you use abs()?  You know that a >= mu1, mu1 >= mu2, etc. so you could just do "a-mu1", etc.
> 3) You use round() both in the nimble model code and in the function.
>
> -chris
>
> On Thu, Mar 11, 2021 at 2:42 AM Enrico Ryunosuke Crema <enrico...@gmail.com> wrote:
> >
> > Dear All,
> >
> > I’m getting a ‘caught segfault -memory not mapped' error when using a custom distribution model and the stick_breaking() function in nimble. The models in the example below are a simplified version of what I am trying to achieve (I do realise there are better ways - e.g. using a Poisson model, but this cannot be done for a number of reasons). Both dTripleExponentialGrowth and dQuadrupleExponentialGrowth basically describe the probability of observing an event at a discrete time t given an exponential growth process where the growth rate has change points (2 and 3). My idea was to use the stick breaking algorithm as the prior of these changepoints. The example below runs perfectly fine with the two changepoint model (dTripleExponentialGrowth) and I am able to correctly estimate the true parameters of my model. However, when trying to fit the three changepoint model (dQuadrupleExponentialGrowth) I get the following error:

I assume this is a problem with my custom model, but the two versions are identical (indeed the plan was to write a generalised N-changepoint model) so I am not sure why one works and the other doesn't. messages.subject: Re: nimble cannot estimate Probit model
messages.subject_clean: nimble cannot estimate Probit model
messages.body_plain:
Hello, thanks for the query.  The fundamental problem going on is the fact that your model only estimates one single "epsilon" term, which is used for every single observation in y.  This is in contrast to your data-generation, which has a separate "error term" for each observation, on the line:

Y = Y+rnorm(N,0,0.75)

where you add a different normally-distributed error to each row of Y.

This can be fixed by changing your model code.  You could either have N different epsilon terms:

spp_code <- nimbleCode({
    for (i in 1:K){
        beta[i] ~ dnorm(0,0.01)
    }

    y_star[1:N] <- x[1:N,1:K]%*%beta[1:K]

    for (j in 1:N){

        epsilon[j] ~ dnorm(0,1)
        y[j] ~ dbern(phi(y_star[j] + epsilon[j]))
    }
})

Or, you could embed the error using a normal distribution.  This is mathematically equivalent to the code above:

spp_code <- nimbleCode({
    for (i in 1:K){
        beta[i] ~ dnorm(0,0.01)
    }

    y_star[1:N] <- x[1:N,1:K]%*%beta[1:K]

    for (j in 1:N){

        y_p[j] ~ dnorm(y_star[j], 1)
        y[j] ~ dbern(phi(y_p[j]))
    }
})

In either case, you'll have to make some changes to your initial values list, since in the first case, epsilon is no longer a scalar, and in the second case, epsilon doesn't even exist (although you might provide initial values for the y_p terms).

Give this a go, and it should accurately estimate the model.  You may also consider a slightly longer burn-in period than 100 iterations, maybe perhaps 500 or 1000.

Cheers,
Daniel

messages.subject: Markov properties related to SMC/particle sampling?
messages.subject_clean: Markov properties related to SMC/particle sampling?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I’ve got a combo of a theoretical/coding question and I’m hoping one you may have some insights.

Say we have a state-space model with Y_t vector of data at time t and X_t latent unobserved states (below example from Michaud paper) with some function f and g.

Y_t ~ g(y_t | x_t, theta)
X_t ~ f(x_t | x_t-1, theta)

I know that f() is specifying the Markov properties of the state-space model (correct me if I’m wrong).

The question I have is that if we use something like SMC or a particle filter does the sampler actually use x_t-1 to estimate the x_t latents states? When I look at the algorithms this does not seem to be the case because the particle filter is estimating the marginal likelihood based on a proposal for theta (for example) and then you can draw the latent states after completing y_1:T (at least this is what I think).I just want to be sure that I know what it’s doing under the hood.

This is related to my previous question because I'm trying to use the accepted latent state (location in my case) to sample for the location of a covariate to use in my model. I don't want it to use x_t-1 to sample the location, I want it to use x_t.

Hopefully this questions makes sense.

Best,
Rowenna

messages.subject_clean: Markov properties related to SMC/particle sampling?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Rowenna,

Thanks for the question.  This sounds like an interesting application.

The particle filters work by simulating many states at each time step.  The states are weighted and/or resampled at each step.  The basic idea of the theory behind using this in PMCMC is that if the Monte Carlo likelihood approximation is unbiased, it can be used in Metropolis-Hastings updates.

I believe that if the latent states are in the monitors (which they will likely not be by default), they will be drawn from particle filter results and put in the model so they can be recorded in the MCMC output.  I guess it would then be the case that other parameters could be updated conditional on the states.  I'm not sure we've tested that case, so please do stay in touch if you try it.  I think the system was written with the idea that all top-level parameters would be sampled by PMCMC (RW_PF) samplers.

I am not sure I follow your last sentence.  Can you explain more if this hasn't addressed your question?

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
Hi Rowenna,

Thanks for the extra explanation.  So x[t] is indexed by time, and it sounds like you are referring to it as being associated with space?  Can you explain more what that means?  That sounds a little unusual, or is this an animal movement model?

Since the x[t]s are not integer-valued, I'm not getting the idea of using them as indices, as in covar1[x[t-1]].

If covar1 does not need to be calculated from the value of x[t-1], you can use something like
x[t] ~ exp(beta0 + beta1*covar1[t-1])
where you provide covar1[t-1], with indices aligned however you need them (offset by one in time, or not, or indexed simply by t if you want).

If covar1 is stochastically related to x[t-1], I think you can make this work by increasing the number of latent states, but I'm not getting what you're trying to do.

If x[t] is a continuous location and you have a discretized grid of locations corresponding to covar1 values, I think you could use something like this:

covar1_index[t-1] <- calculate_grid_index(x[t-1])
x[t] ~ exp(beta0 + beta1*covar1[ covar1_index[t-1] ])

where you would write calculate_grid_index as a nimbleFunction or nimbleRcall or simply model code that converts a continuous location x to an integer index in a grid indexing scheme you would need to set up.  Since you've shown x as one dimensional, I'm not sure of your setup.

That is a bit of a guess but is a kind of application I've seen.

Can you please clarify more if I'm still not getting it.

-Perry

I am working on a bivariate Gaussian Process (point process) model with a user-defined distribution. I am getting the following error when I try to subset the bivariate model to be every other item in the vector.

"Error in parse(text = x, keep.source = FALSE)[[1]] : subscript out of bounds"

I've tried a couple of different methods for extracting every other element. I've sent replication code to Perry and Chris, but happy to send it to anyone else who might be interested in taking look or might be able to help.

I've looked through other similar problems on this group and I might need to use a nimbleFunctionLists, but I'm not sure. I've tried quite a bit of debugging and I think all of the dimensions listed in the code are correct.

Thank you!

Best,
Claire

---
Some more details:
I have a bivariate GP based on a Kronecker product. I would like to extract every other element in this vector. I created a function called subs_gp() that I hoped would accomplish this. I also included the direct subsetting in the "nimbleCode", where wtilda_2 is the GP vector of length 2*n, and w2_int is the vector of indices that is every other number (2,4,6...2*n).

  for(h in 1:n_total){
    w_s2[h] <- wtilda_s[w2_ind[h]]
  }

The problem comes below when I try to add this to a linear regression (the code is below). When I run configureMCMC() with the list of monitors, I get the error referenced above.

  for(i in 1:n_total) {
    logmarks[i] ~ dnorm(mean = va_nonspatial[i] + w_s2[i], sd = lin_sig)
  }

messages.subject: Re: Markov properties related to SMC/particle sampling?
messages.subject_clean: Markov properties related to SMC/particle sampling?
messages.body_plain:
In case anyone was interested in this thread, I'm posting a follow-up on the list.  Rowenna and I continued discussion off-list (accidentally!).  This is a case of an animal movement model where a spatially indexed covariate helps predict where animals will move.  Hence one can set up a spatial grid and use a categorical distribution (dcat) of which grid cell an animal will move to, with the probabilities calculated using the covariate conditional on current location, or one could write a custom distribution to accomplish this.  (A related point is that MCMC sampling with latent states that follow dcat with many categories can be slow because the default sampler will try every category on every iteration, although in this case PMCMC was of interest).

-Perry

>
> If covar1 does not need to be calculated from the value of x[t-1], you can use something like
> x[t] ~ exp(beta0 + beta1*covar1[t-1])

> If x[t] is a continuous location and you have a discretized grid of locations corresponding to covar1 values, I think you could use something like this:
>
> covar1_index[t-1] <- calculate_grid_index(x[t-1])
> x[t] ~ exp(beta0 + beta1*covar1[ covar1_index[t-1] ])
>
> where you would write calculate_grid_index as a nimbleFunction or nimbleRcall or simply model code that converts a continuous location x to an integer index in a grid indexing scheme you would need to set up.  Since you've shown x as one dimensional, I'm not sure of your setup.

messages.body_plain:
hi Claire,

Thanks for this report (and for the off-list reproducible example). It looks like this is a bug on our side.

The problem comes in trying to create conjugate samplers for the elements of alpha and gamma, which involves (via a series fo deterministic expressions) wtilda_s.

If I add full indexing to wtilde_s (i.e., change the final "[ , 1]" to "[1:two_ntotal, 1]", things work on my end:

wtilda_s[1:two_ntotal] <- (knon_prod(expcov(dist_knotuof_nk[1:n_total,1:n_knot], phi=phi, sigma=1), Lambda[1:2,1:2])%*%inverse(knon_prod(expcov(distance_latt[1:n_knot, 1:n_knot], phi=phi, sigma=1), Lambda[1:2,1:2]))%*%W_knot[1:two_nknot])[1:two_ntotal,1]

There is an additional issue, which is that even with the change above, nimble doesn't detect that it could assign conjugate samplers for the alphas and gammas. I haven't tracked down why, but given that, if you want to reduce the time spent in configureMCMC, you might as well skip having nimble check for conjugate samplers by adding "useConjugacy = FALSE" as an additional argument to configureMCMC.

-chris

Whoops, should have waited to respond, as my final comment about the additional issue of not detecting conjugacy was not correct.

The alphas and gammas are also involved in the likelihood for 'one', so NIMBLE should not (and does not) detect conjugacy for the alphas and gammas.

So the only issue is that you need to add the full indexing in defining wtilda_s, and on the nimble side, I have filed an issue for us to fix the issue that lack of full indexing causes an error.

-chris

messages.body_plain:
Hi Fang,

It looks like you will need to write some user-defined distributions. Please see Section 12.2 of the NIMBLE manual and this example <https://r-nimble.org/nimbleExamples/zero_inflated_poisson.html> from our website.

For the improper density proportional to 1/x, it's fine to write the improper "density" function as the "d" function for NIMBLE, though it won't make sense to write a random generation "r" function; you can just let NIMBLE define a dummy placeholder "r" function.

For the density for 'y', you'll need to use the 'pnorm' function, which is available for writing nimbleFunction run code. Again, you can just let NIMBLE define a dummy placeholder "r" function.

-chris

messages.subject_clean: Re-writing code for more efficient running
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

I wrote a (complex) multi-state capture recapture
model incorporating a structural equation model in jags. However, the jags
model does not complete the running process, because it is running into memory
issues (which results in the program to crash or getting memory concerning errors
on the server). This is why I started looking into converting the code to
nimble (that I have not used before) which could maybe handle/run it more
efficiently. I started running the model how it is attached and building the
model took more than a day. I found some suggestions on rewriting the code in
this forum like reducing the number of nodes by using nimbleFunction, writing
user-defined distributions, different indexing (scalar vs vectorized
declaration) and some additional options (e.g. calculate=F, useConjugacy=F). I
was wondering if you could give me some concrete suggestions based on the
attached code? I can also provide the data if necessary.

Thank you very much!

Magali

messages.subject: Re: NAs in the linear predictor
messages.subject_clean: NAs in the linear predictor
messages.body_plain:
Hi Daniel,

I hope I find you well. Did you have time to look into the previous issue?

I managed to reproduce the issue with simulated data (see code bellow). I tested it and the issue can be replicated on two different machines (a windows and a linux one). The model is extremely simple and the issue remains the same. For some reason the "mu[100000]" has a weird behavior ie the first is NA and the rest 0, see code attached.

Thanks in advance!

Best wishes,
Gary

library(tidyr)
library(nimble)

Ncases <- 28271
ncontrols <- c(rep(3, times = 15842), rep(4, times = 12429))

set.seed(11)
ncontrols <- ncontrols[sample(1:length(ncontrols), size = length(ncontrols))]
dat <- data.frame(O = rep("case", times = Ncases), ncontrols = ncontrols, ID = c(1:Ncases))
head(dat)

dat$control1 <- "control1"
dat$control2 <- "control2"
dat$control3 <- "control3"
dat$control4 <- "control4"
dat$control4[dat$ncontrols == 3] <- NA

dat <- dat[,c("ID", "ncontrols", "O", paste0("control", 1:4))]
data_long <- gather(dat, casecontrol, CCflag, O:control4, factor_key=TRUE)
head(data_long)

data_long$casecontrol <- NULL
data_long$O <- 0
data_long$O[data_long$CCflag %in% "case"] <- 1
data_long <- data_long[complete.cases(data_long$CCflag),]
data_long$ncontrols <- NULL

data_long$temperature <- rnorm(n = nrow(data_long), mean = 20, sd = 3)

# now the nimble model

model_1_linear <- nimbleCode(
  {
    for(i in 1:N){

      O[i] ~ dpois(mu[i])

      mu[i] <- exp(b_tmp*temperature[i] + u[IDCC[i]])

    }

    for(j in 1:J){
      u[j] ~ dnorm(0, sd = 100)
    }

    b_tmp ~ dnorm(0, sd = 10)
  }
)

# data
N <- nrow(data_long)
J <- max(data_long$ID)

nimble_data <- list(

  O = data_long$O,
  temperature = data_long$temperature

)

nimble_constants <- list(

  N = N,
  IDCC = data_long$ID,
  J = J

)

initials = list(

  b_tmp = -0.1,
  u = rep(0.1, times = J)

)

parameters <- c("b_tmp", "mu[1]", "mu[100000]", "mu[162]", "u[2]", "u[20]", "u[1662]")

t_0 <- Sys.time()

nimble_model_1 <- nimbleModel(
  code = model_1_linear,
  data = nimble_data,
  constants = nimble_constants,
  inits = initials,
  name = "model_1_linear",
  calculate = FALSE
)

Cmodel_1 <- compileNimble(nimble_model_1)
Cmodel_1$calculate()

nimble_model_1$origInits

conf <- configureMCMC(nimble_model_1, monitors = parameters)
MCMC <- buildMCMC(conf)
cMCMC <- compileNimble(MCMC, project = Cmodel_1)

set.seed(11)
mod1res <- runMCMC(cMCMC, niter = 50000, samples = TRUE, nburnin = 30000, thin = 10)

plot(mod1res[,"mu[1]"])
plot(mod1res[,"mu[100000]"])
plot(mod1res[,"u[1]"])
plot(mod1res[,"b_tmp"])
plot(mod1res[,"u[20]"])
plot(mod1res[,"u[1662]"])

messages.body_plain:
Gosh, Gary, I'm so sorry that we (I) let this question languish on the nimble-users list.  That would be my fault.

Since then, your findings prompted a lengthy behind-the-scenes discussion, and investigation, among the development NIMBLE team.  It was a quandary, because originally I was unable to reproduce the behaviour you were experiencing, while others were.

What it boiled down to, was R's default behaviour of using scientific notation for large (round) numbers, and control of this "feature" using R's "scipen" option which dictates the degree of R's tendency to use scientific notation for large numbers..  For example:

> options('scipen')
$scipen
[1] 0             ## default value of zero
>
> 1000000
[1] 1e+06         ## problem for NIMBLE
>
> options(scipen = 999)
>
> 1000000
[1] 1000000       ## good

As it turned out, I personally had the following line in my .rprofile file, which I'd completely forgotten about (added years ago):

options(scipen=999)  ## turns off scientific notation display

So I wasn't having this problem.  Anyway, two things to say:

1. We've made a fix for this in NIMBLE, how we process numbers (in particular, node indices), and prevent R from using scientific notation when we do processing of node indices (e.g., not allowing "x[1000000]" to be changed, by R, into "x[1e+06]"), and

2. Until this updated NIMBLE release comes out, try executing the command "options(scipen = 999)", and that should clear up the problem for you in the meantime.

Please let me know if this works for you, and again, I'm sorry to have let this question hang for so long.

Cheers,
Daniel

>
> Since then, your findings prompted a lengthy behind-the-scenes discussion, and investigation, among the development NIMBLE team.  It was a quandary, because originally I was unable to reproduce the behaviour you were experiencing, while others were.
>
> What it boiled down to, was R's default behaviour of using scientific notation for large (round) numbers, and control of this "feature" using R's "scipen" option which dictates the degree of R's tendency to use scientific notation for large numbers..  For example:
>
> > options('scipen')
> $scipen
> [1] 0             ## default value of zero
> >
> > 1000000
> [1] 1e+06         ## problem for NIMBLE
> >
> > options(scipen = 999)
> >
> > 1000000
> [1] 1000000       ## good
>
> As it turned out, I personally had the following line in my .rprofile file, which I'd completely forgotten about (added years ago):
>
> options(scipen=999)  ## turns off scientific notation display
>
> So I wasn't having this problem.  Anyway, two things to say:
>
> 1. We've made a fix for this in NIMBLE, how we process numbers (in particular, node indices), and prevent R from using scientific notation when we do processing of node indices (e.g., not allowing "x[1000000]" to be changed, by R, into "x[1e+06]"), and
>
> 2. Until this updated NIMBLE release comes out, try executing the command "options(scipen = 999)", and that should clear up the problem for you in the meantime.

messages.body_plain:
Hi Magali,

Thanks for posting this example.  Here are some suggestions.

Try using "calculate=FALSE" in the call to nimbleModel.  For such a large model, the uncompiled calculation can be a substantial portion of the time.  When you get to configureMCMC, try using "useConjugacy=FALSE" to make that faster.

Try replacing one of the lines like this:
PSI[ 1 , 2 ,i,j]<- phi[1,i,j] * ( SW[j] * (psiSW1[1]/(sum(psiSW1[1:8]) )) + WS[j] * (psiWS1[1]/(sum(psiWS1[1:8]) ))  )

with an arrangement like this:
PSI[ from_state , to_state ,i,j]<- phi[from_state,i,j] * ( SW[to_state] * (psiSW[from_state, to_state]/(sum_psiSW[from_state])) + WS[to_state] * (psiWS[from_state, to_state]/(sum_psiWS[from_state])))
(which would be enclosed an additional for-loops for from_state and to_state)
with the following in an appropriate for-loop
sum_psiSW[from_state] <- sum(psiSW[from_state, 1:8])
sum_psiWS[from_state] <- sum(psiWS[from_state, 1:8])

The reason for creating the sum_psiXX variables is to reduce redundant calculation and simplify the model graph.  The reason to write fewer lines of model code with more indexing is that every line of model code creates overhead.

I would remove the E0 declarations and provide E0 in the constants list.

A big change you could try would be to use the dDHMM (dynamic hidden Markov model) in nimbleEcology, reducing the need for the many individual latent states and sampling of dcat variables, which is typically not very efficient.

Similarly I would change this
log(psiSW1[s]) <- betaSW1[s] # from state 1 in summer -> winter
betaSW1[s] ~ dnorm(0,1)

to
log(psiSW[k, s]) <- betaSW1[k, s] # from state 1 in summer -> winter
betaSW1[k, s] ~ dnorm(0,1)

to avoid embedding indices in variable names and have many fewer declarations.

This is a small thing, but you don't need the taus.  Instead you can use the sigmas, e.g.
cov[i,1] ~ dnorm(mu1[i],  sd = sig1x)

If this still doesn't go well, there are some more in-depth things you could try.  For example, if you don't want to use the dDHMM because you want to sample the individual latent states, you could skip over all of the PSI and E arrays and write a custom distribution that uses the ingredients directly.  It would look something like:

alive[i,j] ~ dMyCRmodel(phi[ alive[i, j-1], i, j],   psiSW[1:9, 1:8], psiWS[1:9, 1:8] ). # I may not have that just right, but the idea is to pass the ingredients as arguments / parent nodes

which internally could use the elements needed without ever forming the large arrays.  (The alive[i,j] should still be sampled by a categorical sampler, but check the configureMCMC output to be sure.)  Some of the slow performance in JAGS or NIMBLE is likely due to the large model graph from the large arrays.  A benefit of NIMBLE's extensibility (you can write new functions and distributions) is to avoid that kind of inefficient (but common) use of the model language.

Separately, or in addition, one could write a sampler that makes use of latent state structure of the model.

I hope some of that helps.  Let us know how it goes.

Perry
